summary: Computing in the Network (COIN) considers running processing on devices like switches and network interface cards. This informational RFC presents use cases and puts such functionality in the context of general Internet communication.

eli5.summary: Usually the network just carries mail. COIN asks if the mail trucks could also do some work on the way. This lists the examples.

subtitle: Applications and opportunities for computing deployed directly in network devices like switches and NICs.

tldr.problem: Networks today are primarily designed for forwarding packets between endpoints. Many emerging applications would benefit from performing computation at intermediate network devices, but the case for such in-network computing capabilities has not been clearly articulated.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC presents six categories of use cases where computing in the network (COIN) could add value: new user experiences (mobile offloading, extended reality, performing arts), enabling new systems (time-sensitive control, large-volume monitoring, industrial safety), improving existing services (content delivery, compute fabrics), and enabling new capabilities (distributed AI training).
tldr.outcome: The document identifies research questions and desirable capabilities needed to support COIN systems. It provides a foundation for the research community to explore how in-network computing could improve network performance, reduce latency, and enable applications that would otherwise be impossible.

today: RFC 9817 is an IRTF Informational RFC published in August 2025. It represents the consensus of the Computing in the Network Research Group and provides a comprehensive foundation for COIN research. The document has been reviewed by experts within and outside COINRG. It is not an IETF standard and makes no claim to protocol specifications; instead, it serves as a research roadmap for the community exploring how computing capabilities can be integrated into network devices to improve performance, latency, and application possibilities.

sections.title: The Vision of In-Network Computing
sections.content:
The Internet was designed as a best-effort packet network with simple forwarding at intermediate nodes and complex processing at endpoints. While this simplicity enabled rapid growth, emerging applications demand more: strict performance guarantees, closed-loop control, and tighter integration of computing and networking.

Computing in the Network (COIN) refers to the deployment of processing functionality on programmable network devices such as switches and network interface cards. This vision represents a shift from a telephone-network analogy toward a distributed computer architecture where computation and communication resources are jointly optimized throughout the network.

This document presents use cases organized along four dimensions: those providing new user experiences, enabling new systems, improving existing capabilities, and enabling entirely new capabilities. Each use case discusses the problem, current solutions, opportunities, research questions, and desired capabilities for COIN systems.
sections.eli5: Networks carry messages between computers. COIN asks: what if the switches and network cards could also do useful work on the data as it passes through? What applications would benefit from that?

sections.title: Key Terminology and System Concepts
sections.content:
COIN systems consist of Programmable Network Devices (PNDs) such as switches and network interface cards that can run code (e.g., using P4 or other languages), together with COIN execution environments (e.g., JVM-based runtimes) and the communication resources interconnecting them. A COIN program is a monolithic piece of functionality that can be deployed and instantiated across the system. COIN capabilities are features enabled through joint processing of computation and communication resources.

The document uses a consistent taxonomy for each use case: describing the problem and its context, characterizing the services and interactions involved, surveying existing solutions, outlining opportunities enabled by COIN, identifying research questions that must be addressed, and specifying desirable capabilities beyond those required by the research questions.
sections.eli5: Key concepts include programmable switches, the software environments that run on them, the programs deployed to them, and the capabilities that result from putting computation in the network.

sections.title: Providing New User Experiences
sections.content:
COIN enables three categories of new user experiences. Mobile Application Offloading partitions mobile apps into microservices that can be deployed on edge servers or PNDs. A VR headset's display program might stay local while CPU-intensive content processing runs on a nearby server selected dynamically, improving frame rates and reducing battery drain.

Extended Reality and Immersive Media (VR, AR, MR) demand multistream aggregation at the edge, low latencies, and intelligent caching close to users. COIN enables functional decomposition across fog, edge, and cloud resources. For example, data filtering, video processing, and image rendering can leverage different hardware (CPUs, GPUs) at network edges, reducing the bandwidth and latency that would be required by cloud-only solutions.

Personalized and Interactive Performing Arts involves live performances with geographically distributed performers and audience. COIN programs deployed on-path in PNDs can perform media aggregation, encoding, and personalization (viewpoint selection, subtitles, audio description) without routing streams through centralized servers, maintaining the latency bounds needed for real-time interaction.
sections.eli5: Three examples: a video game offloading heavy computation to nearby servers, virtual reality showing different perspectives to different viewers by processing video at the network edge, and live theater letting remote audiences see the performance from their chosen viewpoint.

sections.title: Supporting New Systems and Domains
sections.content:
COIN enables three new kinds of systems. In-Network Control for Time-Sensitive Applications addresses modern industrial production lines that require centralized control logic but must maintain tight latency bounds (single-digit milliseconds). Deploying simplified control algorithms on PNDs close to machinery provides quick, inaccurate responses while more complex control logic in the cloud provides accuracy at higher latencies, balancing responsiveness and precision.

Large-Volume Data Applications in industrial monitoring produce gigabits per second of sensor data. COIN programs deployed on-premise can filter redundant data, downsample sensors, and perform early aggregation (e.g., finding maximum values) before data leaves the site, reducing bandwidth requirements and protecting business secrets through encryption that COIN operations respect.

Industrial Safety can be enhanced by combining diverse sensor data (worker positions, robot locations, light barriers) in COIN programs on PNDs for early detection of hazardous situations, enabling rapid response without requiring extensive network-level state convergence.
sections.eli5: Three industrial examples: robots that respond quickly to danger by having control logic nearby, factories that reduce data transmission by filtering uninteresting measurements at the network edge, and safety systems that combine sensors to detect hazards early.

sections.title: Improving and Enabling Capabilities
sections.content:
Content Delivery Networks can be improved by COIN-enabled service-level routing that dynamically selects among pool of CDN servers based on current telemetry, constraint-based routing decisions, and in-network multicast for efficient content replication that reduces network and storage utilization.

Compute-Fabric-as-a-Service (CFaaS) provides infrastructure providers with tenant-specific pools of connected compute resources at edges and data centers. COIN enables service-level routing of compute requests, constraint-based resource selection, and in-network enforcement of traffic isolation and trust policies between tenants and providers.

Virtual Network Programming allows tenants to deploy and operate COIN programs (such as P4 code) in their virtual networks over underlying infrastructure like 5G or data centers. This enables unified programming models that can be ported across deployments and new levels of customization for customers.

Distributed AI Training is enabled by COIN through efficient collective communication primitives (all-to-all, scatter-gather) executed in network-placed COIN programs, and service-level routing of training requests to appropriate worker nodes, improving both network and compute utilization.
sections.eli5: Four examples: CDNs becoming smarter about which cache to use, multiple companies sharing data center compute while staying isolated from each other, tenants programming their own network behavior, and distributed AI systems using the network to efficiently combine results from multiple workers.

sections.title: Research Questions and Categorization
sections.content:
The document identifies dozens of research questions organized into five categories. Vision questions address where computation should be placed and which tasks are suitable for COIN. Enabling Technologies questions focus on what technologies are needed to make COIN reality, including interoperability and integration with existing systems. Distributed Computing Frameworks questions concern deployment, orchestration, composition, and operation of COIN programs.

Applicability Areas are use-case-specific categories: Transport addresses protocol adaptation for dynamic deployment; App Design concerns principles for COIN applications; Data Processing covers handling and analysis in COIN environments; Routing and Forwarding explores efficient mechanisms; and Industrial Control addresses real-time systems, automation, and fault tolerance.

Security considerations note that COIN systems inherit middlebox security challenges: PNDs typically lack cryptography support and work on unencrypted data, raising privacy concerns and attack surface issues. Research on granting middleboxes access to secured traffic remains in its infancy, with approaches ranging from SplitTLS to searchable encryption to the industrial-domain MADTLS protocol.
sections.eli5: Big research questions fall into categories: where should computation go, what technologies are needed, how should programs be managed, and how do you solve domain-specific problems safely.
